head: Code
What it does
When to reach for it
rows: Append the first k−1 tiles at the end
Unrolls the circle: every circular window of k tiles is an ordinary window in `ext`
Length of the current alternating run ending at i
Resets to 1 when two neighbours have the same colour
A window of k alternating tiles ends at i
Every position with a long enough run closes exactly one group

blocks.h: Why is the extension only k − 1 long?
p: A circular window starting at index s ≤ n−1 needs tiles s … s+k−1 (mod n), i.e. at most n+k−2 as an index in the unrolled array. Appending k−1 tiles covers all of them without counting any group twice. Each end position i with a run of at least k contributes one group, so a long run of length L gives L−k+1 groups.

3208.takeaway: Unroll the circle by appending k−1 tiles and count end positions whose alternating run has length at least k.

O(1) membership instead of scanning nums for every node
Start of the output list and its tail pointer
Build a new chain of kept nodes
Append the current node to the kept list
The last kept node may still point to a removed node

p: Suppose the list ends with removed nodes (e.g. `4→5→1` with 1 removed). The last kept node, 5, still points to 1 because we never changed its `next`. Setting `tail.next = None` cuts that stale link. Without a dummy node, handling a removed head would need a special case.

3217.takeaway: Rebuild the list from kept nodes using a dummy head and a tail pointer; terminate the tail and use a set for lookups.

head: Code
What it does
When to reach for it
rows: Only the count of each letter matters
Odd count leaves 1 character, even count leaves 2
Each operation removes two copies of a letter (one on each side of a middle one)

p: `'abaacbcbb'` → 5:

An operation needs a letter with a copy on each side and deletes those two neighbours, so a letter with 3 or more copies loses 2 each time. A letter can be reduced until 1 copy (odd count) or 2 copies (even count) remain: with 2 copies there is no middle one, so no further operation. The positions do not matter because the closest left and right copies can always be arranged for a letter with at least 3 occurrences.

3223.takeaway: Each operation removes two copies of a letter with at least three: odd counts shrink to 1, even counts to 2.

Number of message words that are banned

p: message `['hello', 'world', 'leetcode']`, banned `['world', 'hello']`:

Without it, each word would be searched in the list of banned words (O(m) each, O(n·m) total). A set makes every membership test O(1). Repeated banned words in the message count separately (the sum counts occurrences), as the rule is about words of the message.

3295.takeaway: Put banned words in a set and count how many message words are in it.

head: Code
What it does
When to reach for it
rows: `ord('a') = 97`; subtract, add one, mod 26, add back
Repeat until the word is long enough

p: The length doubles every operation, so reaching length ≥ k takes only ⌈log₂ k⌉ steps (k ≤ 500 in this problem). A closed form exists: the k-th character equals the number of 1-bits in the binary representation of k−1, as a shift from 'a'. For k = 5, k−1 = 4 = 100₂ has one set bit, so the letter is 'b'.

3304.takeaway: Build the word by repeated doubling with a shifted copy until it has k characters; the answer is its k-th letter.

head: Code
What it does
When to reach for it
rows: Distances from s to every node
BFS (Breadth-First Search) on an unweighted tree
First endpoint A of a diameter (longest path)
Now both endpoints' distances are known
The last node marked from i is a farthest node, and one of the diameter's endpoints is always farthest

p: Path `0-1-2-3`: farthest from node 0 is A = 3, farthest from A is B = 0. Answer [3, 3, 0, 0]:

In a tree, for every node i, a farthest node is an endpoint of a longest path (diameter). So it is enough to compare the distances to the two endpoints and take the larger. Three BFS passes (O(n) each) replace a BFS from every node (O(n²)). The result is a valid farthest node for every i on 200 random trees: True.

3313.takeaway: Find the two endpoints of a diameter with BFS (Breadth-First Search); the farthest node from any i is the endpoint farther from i.

head: Code
What it does
When to reach for it
rows: Difference array: +1 at the start of a query range, −1 just after its end
Counts, for each index, how many queries cover it
`cover` = number of queries covering index i
Fewer queries than the value needs
Each covering query can decrement the element at most once
Fail at the first index that can't reach 0

p: Result False: index 0 is covered by only one query but needs 4.

Using a query lets us decrement any subset of its range by 1. If we apply all queries covering index i we can decrement nums[i] up to `cover[i]` times, and choosing which indexes to decrement in each query is free. So index i can reach 0 iff nums[i] ≤ cover[i]; indexes don't interfere.

3355.takeaway: Difference array counts the queries covering each index; the array can be zeroed iff every nums[i] ≤ cover[i].

head: Code
What it does
When to reach for it
rows: `a` = best sum in u's subtree when u keeps at most k edges to its CHILDREN; `b` = best sum when u keeps at most k−1 child edges (one slot reserved for the edge to its parent)
Start by keeping NO edge to any child, but taking each child's own best (child allowed all k of its child edges)
Gain from keeping the edge (u, v): `w` plus the child's value in the restricted state `b`, minus the child's baseline `a`
Keeping the edge costs the child one slot
Never keep an edge that lowers the total
Keep the k largest gains (and `[: k − 1]` for the restricted state)
Greedy choice of which child edges to keep

p: edges `[[0,1,4],[0,2,2],[2,3,12],[2,4,6]]`, `k = 2` → 22 (delete the weight-2 edge). Nodes finish bottom-up:

A node's edge to its parent consumes one of its k slots. The parent decides whether to keep that edge, so the child must supply both its best value with all k slots free for children (`a`, used when the edge to the parent is deleted) and with one slot reserved (`b`, used when it is kept). The parent compares the two and keeps the k most valuable edges. The result matches a brute-force search over all edge subsets on 200 random trees: True.

bullets: Time: O(n log n): sorting each node's gains.

3367.takeaway: Tree DP with two states per node (all k child slots vs k−1): keep the k most profitable child edges.

head: Code
What it does
When to reach for it
rows: The rectangle's interval along one axis (x: indexes 0, 2; y: indexes 1, 3)
Project each rectangle to a line
This interval starts at or after everything so far ends
A cut can be made at `end`: no rectangle crosses it
Furthest right end among the merged intervals
At least three groups along an axis
Two cuts create three sections, each with at least one rectangle

p: n = 5 with the four rectangles `[[1, 0, 5, 2], [0, 2, 2, 4], [3, 2, 5, 3], [0, 4, 4, 5]]`. Along the y-axis (rows) the sorted intervals `[start, end)` and group counts are:
x-axis groups: 1, y-axis groups: 3 → True (the y-axis gives 3 groups, so two horizontal cuts work).

Rectangles never overlap, but their projections onto one axis can. A cut is valid at a coordinate only if no projection straddles it. Merging overlapping projections into groups leaves exactly the positions where cuts are possible; two cuts need at least three groups, each holding at least one rectangle.

bullets: Time: O(r log r) for sorting r rectangles.

3394.takeaway: Project rectangles on an axis and merge overlapping intervals: three or more groups mean two valid parallel cuts.

head: Code
What it does
When to reach for it
rows: Sort by time; at equal times OFFLINE (False) comes before MESSAGE (True)
Tuple key; `False < True`, so the boolean breaks ties as the problem requires
Time when user u is online again
Take the user offline for 60 units
Duplicates in the list count more than once

p: 2 users, events `[MESSAGE 10 'id1 id0'], [OFFLINE 11 '0'], [MESSAGE 71 'HERE']` → [2, 2]:

blocks.h: Why sort first and process offline events first at ties?
p: Events may arrive in any order, but their effect depends on time: whether a user is online at a message's time depends on earlier OFFLINE events. At the same timestamp the problem says OFFLINE is processed first, so the sort key puts OFFLINE before MESSAGE. Here the HERE message at time 71 reaches user 0 because 11 + 60 = 71 ≤ 71, i.e. the user is back online.

3433.takeaway: Sort events by (time, MESSAGE last), keep each user's back-online time, and apply ALL/HERE/id mentions in order.

head: Code
What it does
When to reach for it
rows: Best total if currently in lane 1 with no switch used
Best total if currently in lane 2 after one switch
Best total if currently in lane 1 again after two switches
State: two switches used (no more allowed)
Either continue in lane 1 or start fresh here
Entering the road at any mile: a new start has total 0
Switch from lane 1 (or start-from-scratch) into lane 2, or stay in lane 2
Lane 2's value `b` is added at this mile
Switch back to lane 1 from lane 2, or stay in lane 1
Best over all states and all end miles
The trip must cover at least one mile, so the maximum is taken after adding a mile

p: The rules limit switches to two and require starting in lane 1, so the lane and the number of switches used form a small state machine: (lane 1, 0 switches), (lane 2, 1 switch), (lane 1, 2 switches). At each mile the best total for each state comes from staying in it or from the previous state by one switch. Starting anywhere is handled by `max(f00, 0)`. The DP agrees with a brute-force search over all start/end miles and lane sequences (entering lane 1 and switching immediately counts as one of the two switches) on 100 random small inputs: True.

3466.takeaway: Small state-machine DP: (lane 1, 0 switches), (lane 2, 1 switch), (lane 1, 2 switches), with a fresh start allowed at every mile.

Sparse: unset cells are 0 by default
The `None` default avoids a KeyError when the cell was never set
Drop the leading `=` and split the two operands

Value of a cell, or 0 if never set

p: Calls in order:

blocks.h: Why a dictionary instead of a 26-column grid?
p: A grid with up to 10⁴ rows × 26 columns would use hundreds of thousands of entries, most of them 0. A dictionary stores only cells that were set; reading a missing cell with `.get(part, 0)` gives the default. Resetting simply removes the key, restoring the default.

bullets: Time: O(1) per call (the formula has a fixed shape X+Y).

3484.takeaway: Sparse dictionary of set cells with a default of 0; parse '=X+Y' by splitting on '+' and telling numbers from cell names.

head: Code
What it does
When to reach for it
rows: FIFO (First In, First Out): the oldest is on the left
Packets are identical if all three match
Timestamps of ALL packets ever added for that destination, in arrival order
Arrival order is non-decreasing in time, so the list stays sorted
How many of destination d's packets have already left the router
The valid packets of d are `ts[d][head[d]:]`
Count timestamps in [start, end] among the packets still stored
`bisect_*` with a third argument `lo = h` ignores the removed prefix

p: `Router(3)`:

blocks.h: Why a per-destination list and a head pointer?
p: Each destination's timestamps are appended in non-decreasing order (the problem guarantees increasing timestamps), so they form a sorted list. Packets leave the router oldest first, and for a given destination the oldest are always the earliest in its list, so removal just moves `head[d]` forward (no deletion from the middle of a list). Counting packets in a time range is then two binary searches in the remaining part. The implementation matches a naive list-based reference on 300 random operation sequences with non-decreasing timestamps (as the problem guarantees): True.

bullets: Time: addPacket, forwardPacket O(1) amortised; getCount O(log n).
Space: O(memoryLimit) for the queue, O(packets ever added) for the timestamp lists.

3508.takeaway: FIFO deque + duplicate set + per-destination timestamp lists with a head pointer, and bisect for range counts.

head: Code
What it does
When to reach for it
rows: The reverse conversion uses the modular inverse of f
`pow(f, MOD−2, MOD)` is f⁻¹ because MOD is prime (Fermat's little theorem)
How many units of v equal one unit of the root unit 0
Everything is expressed relative to node 0
Product of factors on the path from 0
Doubles as the visited check; works because a ratio is never 0 modulo the prime
Converting a to b: one a = ratio[b] / ratio[a] units of b

p: In a tree there is one path between any two units. Converting a to b equals converting a to the root and then the root to b, so `value(b)/value(a)` in terms of the root unit. Computing every unit's factor relative to node 0 once (O(n)) turns each query into a single modular division (a modular inverse by fast exponentiation).

3535.takeaway: Express every unit relative to the root with modular products along tree edges; a query is ratio[b] × inverse(ratio[a]).

When to reach for it

Build the grids from the cables
Per grid, the list of its stations (already ascending)
An ascending list is already a valid min-heap
Lazy deletion: discard offline stations at the top
Only the top matters, so cleanup happens when needed
The answer for an offline query station

head: Query
Answer
What happens
rows: x offline → smallest online in its grid (discarded 1 offline from the heap top)
x offline → smallest online in its grid (discarded 1 offline from the heap top)

p: Stations only go offline (never back), so once a station is offline it can never be the answer again. Removing it from a heap immediately would cost O(n); instead, offline stations are discarded only when they reach the top. Each station is popped at most once overall, which keeps the total at O((c + q) log c).

bullets: Time: O((c + q) · α + c log c).

3607.takeaway: Union-Find for grids plus a lazily cleaned min-heap per grid for the smallest online station.

head: Code
What it does
When to reach for it
rows: Starts at n; each successful union reduces it by one
The last edge used is the heaviest one needed
Every node can be its own component
No edges are needed at all

blocks.h: Why Kruskal until k components remain?
p: To keep at most k components we must keep at least n−k edges forming a forest. To minimise the heaviest kept edge, use the cheapest edges that connect nodes: Kruskal adds edges in increasing weight, and stops as soon as the number of components drops to k. The weight of the last accepted edge is the smallest possible maximum (the bottleneck). The heaviest edge (6) is deleted.

3613.takeaway: Kruskal in increasing weight order, stopping when k components remain: the last accepted edge's weight is the answer.

head: Code
What it does
When to reach for it
rows: Each cell is added to exactly one island
Avoids recursion depth limits on large islands
Sum the island's values as cells are popped

p: Marking a cell visited when it is pushed (not when it is popped) guarantees each cell enters the stack once. The flood fill visits every cell of the island once, so the total work over all islands is O(m·n).

3619.takeaway: Flood-fill each island with a stack, sum its cells, and count totals divisible by k.

head: Code
What it does
When to reach for it
rows: Within a sorted window the minimum is on the left and the maximum on the right
Shrink from the left (raise the minimum)
Everything outside the best window is removed

blocks.h: Why does a contiguous sorted window suffice?
p: A balanced remaining set has some minimum and maximum; all elements between them in sorted order can be kept without breaking the condition, so the optimal kept set is a contiguous block of the sorted array. The largest such block with max ≤ k·min minimises removals.

3634.takeaway: Sort, then slide a window while the maximum is at most k × the minimum; the answer is n minus the longest window.

head: Code
What it does
When to reach for it
rows: The condition depends only on |a| and |b|, and positions only matter through i < j, which is symmetric for pair counting
The smaller value is less than half of the larger
Then the pair is NOT perfect
First index whose value is at least half of `a[i]`
All indexes between j and i−1 pair perfectly with i

p: `[0,1,2,3]` → absolute values `[0, 1, 2, 3]` → 2 pairs:

Both conditions simplify (for x = |a| ≤ y = |b|): min(|a−b|,|a+b|) = y − x and max(...) = y + x, and the conditions become y − x ≤ x and y + x ≥ y, i.e. y ≤ 2x. So a pair is perfect exactly when the larger absolute value is at most twice the smaller. The two-pointer count over the sorted absolute values agrees with a brute-force check of the original definition on 300 random arrays: True.

3649.takeaway: A pair is perfect iff the larger absolute value is at most twice the smaller: sort absolute values and count with two pointers.

head: Code
What it does
When to reach for it
rows: Profit with no modification: Σ strategy[i] · prices[i]
Profit of any range in O(1)
Sum of prices over a range
Remove the old profit of the window
Everything in the window is overwritten
New profit of the window: the second half sells (strategy 1 × price) and the first half holds (0)
Sum of the last k/2 prices
Best change over all windows; 0 means no modification

p: prices `[4,2,8]`, strategy `[-1,0,1]`, `k = 2`: base profit 4; each window's change and the final answer 10:

For each of the n−k+1 windows the profit change is (new profit of the window) − (old profit of the window). Both are range sums, which two prefix-sum arrays give in O(1), so the total is O(n) instead of O(n·k). The result equals a brute-force try of every window on 300 random cases: True.

3652.takeaway: Profit change of a window = new profit (second half sells) − old profit, both from prefix sums; take the best window and add it to the base.
